The argument fails on three levels: it uses a criterion morally irrelevant to what's at stake (suffering), it's inaccurate about animal minds and, applied consistently, it would strip moral protection from millions of human beings.
"Animals aren't rational, so there's no problem using them."

In the philosophical tradition, the argument comes from Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Descartes and Kant; today it appears, for example, in the contractualism of Peter Carruthers. Charitably reconstructed, it goes like this:
Only rational beings (capable of abstract reasoning, deliberation and self-reflection) have full moral status, that is, interests that create direct duties for us.
Non-human animals aren't rational in this sense.
So non-human animals don't have full moral status.
If a being lacks full moral status, it's permissible to use it for important human ends, provided there's no gratuitous cruelty.
So it's permissible to use animals for food, clothing and research.
: rationality wouldn't be a condition for having some moral status, but would give human interests much greater weight. Both versions are dealt with in this chapter.
: if the premises were true, the conclusions would follow. The problem lies in its
: P1, P2 and P3 are false or lack sufficient justification.
The same argument appears in other guises. Recognizing it is the first step to not just answering the surface.
"Animals act on instinct; they don't think."
"You can't compare a human being to an animal."
"Chickens have brains the size of a pea."
"Let me know when a pig writes a book."
"If they were intelligent, wouldn't they build cities?"
"Do you really think a fish thinks?"
"Only rational agents are ends in themselves; other beings have only relative value."
"Morality is an agreement among beings able to understand and follow rules."
"They aren't self-aware." (swaps rationality for self-awareness, with the same problem)

Imagine your friend falls and scrapes their knee. They cry because it hurts, not because they can do sums. It's the same with a dog, a pig or a chicken: they also feel pain, fear and joy, even though they can't read. A baby can't do sums yet either, and no one thinks it's right to hurt them. To know whether we can hurt someone, the question isn't "are they clever?" but "can they feel?".

The moral question isn't whether a being can reason, but whether it can suffer. A pig's pain doesn't hurt less because the pig can't solve equations. If rationality were the criterion, babies and people with profound intellectual disabilities could also be used, and no one accepts that. Besides, the divide "rational humans, irrational animals" is false: crows make hooks to get food, and fish work out social hierarchies just by watching other fish.
"If there were a human being as little rational as a pig, would it be acceptable to raise them for food? If not, what really protects that human?"

As we've seen, the argument is formally valid. So it has to be assessed premise by premise. Three points give way: the normative criterion (P1), the empirical claim (P2) and the bridge between status and use (P3). Before them comes an earlier problem: the word "rational" is ambiguous, and the ambiguity creates a dilemma.
abstract reasoning, propositional language, the ability to reflect on one's own reasons.
learning, making inferences, solving new problems and adjusting behavior to goals.

There's no sense of "rational" that makes P1 and P2 true at the same time without excluding humans whom the speaker protects. Those who use the argument usually switch between the two senses without noticing: the strong one to exclude animals, the weak one to include all humans.

text.bold: 1. The criterion is irrelevant to what's at stake (P1).

paragraph.text: A characteristic only justifies different treatment if it relates to the interest affected. Requiring political understanding in order to vote can be debated; requiring political understanding in order not to be beaten is absurd. Rationality is relevant to some interests, such as political autonomy and moral responsibility, but not to the interest in not feeling pain, fear or deprivation. Jeremy Bentham summed this up in 1789: "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?"

From here comes the sentientist foundation. Having interests means being able to be affected, for better or worse, from the point of view of whoever lives the experience. A stone has no interests; a pig does. That's why sentience is a necessary and sufficient condition for moral inclusion, and the principle of equal consideration of interests (Singer) requires that similar pains count similarly. The criterion is also the most
: a single trait explains why we protect adults, babies, people with dementia and, already today, dogs and cats.

The argument is old: it appears in Porphyry, in the third century, and in Bentham. Today it's called the argument from species overlap (Horta, 2014), a name replacing the older "argument from marginal cases". In the form of
If rationality is necessary for full moral status, then humans without rationality don't have full moral status.
Humans without rationality (newborns, people with profound intellectual disabilities, people with advanced dementia) have full moral status.
So rationality isn't necessary for full moral status.

Q2 is accepted by the speaker. The argument doesn't propose downgrading these humans: it shows the criterion is wrong and that the moral community should be widened, not narrowed (Naconecy). The usual escape routes have their own chapters: the "species norm" (A18) judges individuals by what others have; "potential" (A19) doesn't cover those who will never have rationality; "special relationships" (A12) make protection depend on someone caring.

text.bold: 3. The empirical premise is a caricature (P2).

paragraph.text: As early as 1871, Darwin held that the mental difference between humans and other animals is one of degree, not kind. Research in animal cognition has confirmed this gradual picture (see the table in c). An honest caveat is needed here: citing animal intelligence helps undo the false "rational versus irrational" divide, but using it as the

is a trap. It would mean accepting the speaker's criterion and concluding that chickens or fish, supposedly less intelligent, matter less. The argument against exploitation doesn't depend on animals being intelligent; it depends on their being sentient.

text.bold: 4. The bridge between status and use doesn't hold (P3).

paragraph.text: Even in the moderate version, where rationality would give human interests more weight, the argument doesn't reach its conclusion. First, that extra weight would have to be enormous to outweigh intense, prolonged suffering, plus death, in exchange for taste and convenience, since there are alternatives (J5). Second, the "important human ends" of P3 are, in practice, mostly preferences, not needs. Third, in the Kantian version, duties toward animals are only indirect: cruelty would be wrong because it hardens human character. It follows that torturing a dog in secret, with no effect on anyone, wouldn't be wrong in itself, a conclusion almost no one accepts.

The overall picture is one of continuity, with capacities unevenly distributed among species. None of these data, however, is needed for the moral conclusion: the evidence of sentience, which is far more robust than the evidence of complex reasoning, is enough.

The philosophically strongest version comes from contractualism, defended on this subject by Peter Carruthers (1992). Morality would be the set of rules that rational agents would accept in order to live together. Only those who can understand, accept and follow rules are party to the contract. Animals would be left out and would have, at most, indirect protection, because cruelty reveals bad character. Non-rational humans would be included for two reasons: the contractors care about them, and excluding them would create social insecurity, since anyone could come to lose their rationality. A close variant, Carl Cohen's, grants rights through membership of a species of moral agents and is dealt with in chapter A18.

text.bold: It confuses who makes the rules with whom the rules protect.

paragraph.text: Moral agents are those who can have duties; moral patients are those who can be harmed. Babies are patients without being agents, and no one concludes that their protection is therefore a favor.

text.bold: It makes the protection of vulnerable humans contingent.

paragraph.text: If a baby is protected only because the contractors care about them, then torturing an orphan nobody cares about wouldn't be wrong in itself. The theory fails precisely the test of our firmest moral judgments.

text.bold: The contract's own device points the other way.

paragraph.text: Behind Rawls's veil of ignorance, rules are chosen without knowing what position one will occupy. Mark Rowlands (1997) observed that if we also didn't know whether we'd be human or some other sentient being, we'd choose rules protecting all sentient beings. Excluding animals only appears when the contract is designed by those who already have power, and power isn't justice (A9).

text.bold: Even if accepted, it doesn't justify the real practice.

paragraph.text: Contractualism itself condemns cruelty; large-scale farming and slaughter systems, with confinement and mutilation, would hardly pass even that minimal filter.

paragraph.text: The universalization test applies the principle "whoever isn't rational may be used" to other cases. If the person rejects the consequences, they must abandon or reformulate the principle.

They could undergo painful procedures without anesthesia. A newborn doesn't reason, speak or reflect on themselves. If protection from pain depends on rationality, they'd have no right to it, and the fact that they feel pain would be irrelevant
Not just hypothetical: until the 1980s, surgery on newborns was performed with minimal anesthesia in the belief that they didn't really feel pain, a practice revised after Anand and Hickey (1987)
People with profound intellectual disabilities or advanced dementia

They could be used as test subjects or organ sources. These people will never have, or have lost, the rationality the criterion demands. The criterion offers no reason to protect them, and the care we give them would stop being a duty and become a favor
A conclusion rejected by practically everyone

The appeal to capacities wouldn't only decide who deserves respect, but also how much. If what matters is rationality or intelligence, and it varies in degree, there'd be a moral scale among humans: a person with a doctorate would be worth more than someone who can barely read, and their interests would take priority in a conflict
This is exactly what happened: Aristotle attributed incomplete reason to "natural slaves" and women, and colonial discourse called whole peoples "irrational" to justify domination

A being far more rational than us could use us as we use animals. If superior rationality gives the right to use the less rational, the distance between us and that being would justify the same treatment we give a pig today, and we'd have nothing to complain about
Whoever rejects this conclusion is, in practice, appealing to sentience

Torturing an animal without witnesses would only be bad because of the habit it creates. In the Kantian version, the animal isn't a victim: the duty is only to humanity. If no one knew and the torturer went on treating people well, there'd be nothing wrong at all
Contradicts the common intuition that the wrong lies in what is done to the victim

Rationality does have moral importance, but elsewhere. It's relevant to goods such as autonomy, political rights and responsibility: animals aren't moral agents, and a lion commits no crime by hunting. Cognitive differences can also change

harms each being; a being with long-term plans may lose more by dying (McMahan's time-relative interest account, 2002). Finally, equal consideration isn't identical treatment: a pig doesn't need the right to vote.
What the argument can't show is the decisive step: rationality can adjust the
of our duties, but it doesn't decide
the moral circle. That role belongs to sentience.
